name: Barbados
summary: A British sugar colony from 1627, independent in 1966; became a republic in 2021.

knownFor.label: Rum
knownFor.note: Mount Gay, one of the oldest rum makers.

knownFor.label: Cricket
knownFor.note: Great players such as Garfield Sobers.

location.value: Atlantic Ocean, Lesser Antilles, the southern and easternmost island of the Caribbean region; area 439 km².

terrain.value: A flat island of coral limestone, with gentle hills and no rivers.

climate.value: Tropical, with a hurricane season, though the island lies at the edge of the storm belt.

disasters.value: Hurricanes, and droughts that stress the island’s limited fresh water.

population.value: 269,090 at the 2021 census; 281,998 in a 2023 estimate.

urbanisation.value: Bridgetown, the capital, and the southern and western coasts are the most built-up.

migration.value: Large emigration to the UK, US and Canada.

economicBase.value: Historically sugarcane; diversified into manufacturing and tourism from the late 1970s and early 1980s. Tourism is a leading sector, and offshore finance and information services are important earners.

tradeRoutes.value: The Bridgetown port handles cruise ships and cargo.

wealth.value: A high-income economy, based on tourism and financial services.

moneyAndTax.value: The Barbadian dollar, pegged to the US dollar at 2 to 1.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A republic within the Commonwealth since 30 November 2021, when Sandra Mason took office as its first president.

keyRulers.value: Errol Barrow became premier after the 1961 election and first prime minister at independence on 30 November 1966. Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: Elections choose the prime minister; since 2021 the head of state is a president.

institutions.value: One of the oldest parliaments in the Americas (1639).

stability.value: A stable democracy since independence in 1966.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Police and a small defence or coast-guard force.

majorWars.value: No war of independence. Civil-war-era fighting reached the island (an invasion force arrived in October 1651; Royalists surrendered on 11 January 1652), and in 1983 Barbados let the US use it as a launchpad for the invasion of Grenada.

alliancesRivals.value: A member of the Commonwealth and CARICOM.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Schools; University of the West Indies campuses nearby.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Good roads and a busy airport; there are no railways.

religion.value: 75.6% Christian and 20.6% no religion in 2020 (infobox), but the 2021 census put no religion at 45.5%, so the figures conflict.

languageWriting.value: English is official; Bajan, an English-based Creole, is widely spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Crop Over festival; Historic Bridgetown (World Heritage Site).

socialStructure.value: Mostly of African descent, from people enslaved on sugar plantations.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Barbadian identity, with pride in cricket and the Crop Over festival.

dailyLife.value: Houses; fish, breadfruit, rice and peas.

neighbours.value: Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent, to the west.

colonisation.value: A British colony from 1627 until independence in 1966.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge. The economy diversified into tourism and manufacturing from the late 1970s and early 1980s; tourism and offshore finance are major earners.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence: independent since 30 November 1966 and a republic within the Commonwealth since 30 November 2021.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
